Gaussian integrals and convolution

Convolution lets us formulate a central limit theorem directly in terms of functions and their integral actions. The first checked addition is the finite algebra and quantitative replacement estimate that such a proof needs.

Current scope. The convolution and replacement theorems below are checked Lean results over finite rational kernels. The full Gaussian integral, its identification with geometric \(\pi\), and a continuous central limit theorem remain targets. No Mathlib real numbers are imported.

Convolution adds locations and multiplies weights

Checked

A finite kernel consists of rational locations \(x_i\) and nonnegative rational weights \(p_i\) whose sum is one. Its action on a function is

\[A_K(h)=\sum_i p_i h(x_i).\]

Convolution constructs every pair \((x_i+y_j,p_iq_j)\). Finite interchange proves commutativity and associativity of the action. No equality of list encodings is required.

\[A_{K*L}(h)=\sum_i p_i\sum_jq_jh(x_i+y_j).\]

The resulting kernel has mass one. Means and variances add:

\[\mu_{K*L}=\mu_K+\mu_L,\qquad v_{K*L}=v_K+v_L.\]

Writing \(T_Kh(x)=\sum_i p_i h(x-x_i)\), the function composition law is \(T_{K*L}h=T_K(T_Lh)\). Repeating convolution gives \(\mu_{K^{*n}}=n\mu_K\) and \(v_{K^{*n}}=nv_K\).

Lean definitions and proofs

Matching moments cancel the quadratic part

Checked

If two kernels have equal means and second moments, they agree on every quadratic test function. A cubic remainder therefore controls the change when one kernel replaces the other.

\[|h(x)-P(x)|\le C|x|^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |A_K(h)-A_L(h)|\le C\bigl(\rho_3(K)+\rho_3(L)\bigr),\]

Here \(P\) is quadratic and \(\rho_3(K)=\sum_i p_i|x_i|^3\). The bound is required only on the actual supports.

The repeated replacement theorem takes a common local quadratic \(P_z\) at every rational translation, with

\[|h(z+rx)-P_z(x)|\le C|r|^3|x|^3.\]

Replacing one convolution factor at a time proves the explicit estimate

\[\left|A_{K^{*n}}(h(r\,\cdot))-A_{L^{*n}}(h(r\,\cdot))\right|\le nC|r|^3\bigl(\rho_3(K)+\rho_3(L)\bigr).\]

For \(n=m^2\) and \(r=1/m\), the coefficient is \(C/m\). This is a completely rational instance of the central-limit scaling. General represented scales, continuous integration, and Gaussian stability still need their own proofs.

The public theorem is scaled_convolutionPower_cubic_bound. Its hypotheses supply pointwise remainder bounds; its conclusion is derived by finite moment cancellation and telescoping.

An exact check that moments do not determine a law

Checked examples
\[K=\tfrac12\delta_{-1}+\tfrac12\delta_1,\qquad L=\tfrac18\delta_{-2}+\tfrac34\delta_0+\tfrac18\delta_2.\]

Both kernels have mean zero and variance one. Their fourth moments are \(1\) and \(4\), so the laws differ. Their absolute third moments are \(1\) and \(2\), providing concrete replacement budgets.

The literal evaluator also checks that \(K^{*4}\) has variance \(4\) and fourth moment \(40\). Rescaling its locations by \(1/2\) restores variance one.

Exact examples and axiom audit

The Gaussian identities to construct next

Targets

The working-tree Gaussian program already contains rational bounded quadrature, tail estimates and a valid full-line candidate. Connecting that candidate to justified compact integrals and their exhaustion remains an explicit obligation. Its normalization must be proved against the existing geometric \(\pi\).

A direct normalization route uses the rational slope substitution \(y=tx\) on a triangle. For \(I_R=\int_{-R}^R e^{-x^2}\,dx\), the identity to formalize is

\[I_R^2\simeq4\int_0^1\frac{1-e^{-(1+t^2)R^2}}{1+t^2}\,dt.\]

The finite square decomposition and diagonal error bound are now checked: for cell masses \(a_i\), \( (\sum_i a_i)^2=2\sum_{i<j}a_ia_j+\sum_i a_i^2\), and \(0\le a_i\le\delta\) implies \(\sum_i a_i^2\le\delta\sum_i a_i\). The ball-volume and Gamma page explains these new lemmas and provides an exact rational volume calculator.

The established arctangent normalization then gives \(0\le\pi-I_R^2\le4e^{-R^2}\le4/R^2\) for \(R>0\). A finite double-sum comparison must justify the triangular substitution and its degenerate origin edge. This bounded identity is a proof plan, not yet a checked theorem.

With arbitrary valid represented parameters and \(a>0\), the central closed-form target is

\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-ax^2+bx+c}\,dx\simeq\sqrt{\frac\pi a}\,e^{c+b^2/(4a)}.\]

Certified affine substitution then supports shifted and scaled variants. Polynomial-weighted tails and integration by parts give the moment formulas. Completing the square in a justified convolution should prove the heat semigroup law:

\[G_t(x)=\frac{e^{-x^2/(4t)}}{\sqrt{4\pi t}},\qquad G_s*G_t\simeq G_{s+t}\quad(s,t>0).\]

The corresponding Fourier target, with phase \(e^{-i\xi x}\), is \(\widehat G_t(\xi)\simeq e^{-t\xi^2}\). A real completing-the-square formula alone does not justify a complex contour shift.

A central limit theorem about functions

Target

Supply a nonnegative density \(f\) with justified mass, mean and variance integrals equal to \(1\), \(0\) and \(1\). The normalized convolution density is

\[f_n(x)=\sqrt n\,f^{*n}(\sqrt n\,x).\]

The first target is convergence against smooth bounded test functions:

\[\int h(x)f_n(x)\,dx\longrightarrow\int h(x)\frac{e^{-x^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,dx.\]

This is distinct from pointwise convergence of the densities. For a supplied third absolute moment \(\rho_3\) and bound \(|h'''|\le M\), the quantitative target is

\[\left|\int hf_n-\int h\varphi\right|\le\frac{M}{6\sqrt n}\left(\rho_3+2\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\right),\qquad\varphi(x)=\frac{e^{-x^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}.\]

The finite theorem proves the cancellation and accumulation of replacement errors. To obtain this continuous result we still need the cubic Taylor remainder, Gaussian moments and stability, represented scaling, and a scheduled quadrature comparison for the entire replacement sum.

For finite variance without a third moment, a supplied second-moment tail modulus gives an effective truncation schedule. Finiteness of variance alone does not furnish that algorithm.

Mathematical references: Dembo, probability notes, Section 3.1; Chatterjee, the Lindeberg principle. These sources guide the intended proof; they are not imported foundations.
